name: Racket
license: MIT or Apache 2.0, at your option
summary: A descendant of Scheme built for language-oriented programming: every module names its language on a `#lang` line, and new languages are just libraries.
intro: Every Racket module starts with a `#lang` line that names the language the rest of the file is written in: `#lang racket` for the main language, `#lang typed/racket` for its statically typed sibling, a teaching language for beginners, or a domain-specific language someone wrote. A language is itself a module that exports syntax and functions, so it can add features to an existing language, remove them, or even change what function application means. Macros, built on Scheme’s hygienic macro system, are the everyday tool for this.

Racket CS, the default implementation since Racket 8.0 (February 2021), uses Chez Scheme as its core compiler and runtime. Compiled modules (`.zo` files) contain machine code for the operating system and processor, not bytecode. The older implementation, Racket BC (“before Chez”), stored platform-independent bytecode and compiled it to machine code just in time. Racket comes with DrRacket, an IDE that grew out of the project’s teaching roots.
strengths: Language-oriented programming: build a small language for a problem and use it from ordinary Racket modules through `#lang`
A spectrum of safety in one system: Typed Racket, Racket with contracts, plain Racket and unsafe foreign calls can be mixed module by module
Ahead-of-time compilation to machine code through Chez Scheme, which made Racket faster and easier to maintain than the old bytecode implementation
Built for teaching from the start: beginner languages and the DrRacket IDE were the project’s first goals
limits: The syntax extension system makes experts very productive but has, in its own designers’ words, an extraordinarily steep learning curve and some brittle corners
A new language doesn’t get full IDE support for free: tools such as a stepper take significant extra work
Code that calls C through the foreign function interface can behave differently between the CS and BC implementations

story: In 1995 the PLT group (Matthias Felleisen, Robert Bruce Findler, Matthew Flatt, Shriram Krishnamurthi and others) set out to build an outreach project for novice programmers. After a year of watching students in labs, they concluded that nobody could teach Scheme in an hour and then move on to the essence of programming, and that editors like Emacs and vi overwhelmed beginners. They needed teaching languages and a beginner-friendly environment, and built both in Scheme, whose macros helped them experiment with language designs.

Building a large system pushed them past standard Scheme. They added a syntax extension system on top of Scheme’s macros, mechanisms for safe abstractions, and language constructs for managing resources and security. The result, long called PLT Scheme, was renamed Racket with version 5.0 in June 2010, because the word “Scheme” suggested a minimal language it no longer was.
In 2017 the team decided to rebuild Racket on Chez Scheme, which compiles to machine code. After four years of work, Racket CS became the default in version 8.0 in February 2021.

choices.why: Programming happens in the context of a problem with its own vocabulary, so the designers wanted programmers to capture that vocabulary as a programming language, starting with their own teaching languages.
Macros alone could extend a language but not restrict or redefine it. Racket’s system defines whole languages, down to the meaning of function application.

choices.choice: Turn system features into language constructs
choices.why: Running student programs inside their own IDE needed control over resources and security, which Scheme didn’t provide, so Racket made those mechanisms part of the language.
Racket BC had a compiler, JIT and runtime written in C. Rebuilding on Chez Scheme, which compiles to machine code, produced Racket CS: faster, and easier to maintain and develop.

timeline.text: The PLT group starts an outreach project for novice programmers
PLT Scheme is renamed Racket with version 5.0, released in June
Work begins on running Racket on Chez Scheme
Racket 8.0 makes Racket CS the default implementation
